details.title: MA342 - Topology
exam_block: The latest three papers are very similar in structure and topic order; 2025-2026 repeats the four compulsory 25-mark format for a third consecutive year.
Definitions, compactness, connectedness, Hausdorffness, subspace/product/quotient topology and homotopy recur strongly.
The latest paper adds direct evidence for final topology, accumulation-point arguments, connectedness classifications and Cantor-set quotient obstructions.
The current module page learning outcomes align well with the newest papers.
The older papers have a different flavour and were under different starred lecturers.
The exam format changed from 10-question papers to 4 compulsory questions.
The module is proof-heavy, so knowing the topic is not enough; you need clean definitions and precise arguments.
CA is only 30%, which is weaker for the goal of banking coursework marks.
drill: Newer papers emphasise definitions and short proof arguments more than long applications.
Very safe basics: topology definitions, standard/cofinite/discrete topologies, bases, lower-limit topology, neighbourhoods, interiors, closures, accumulation points and density.

Strong preparation target: subspace, initial/final, product and quotient topologies. The 2025-2026 paper explicitly asks for final topology, S1 as a quotient of [0,1] , and whether R can be a quotient of the Cantor set.
Compactness and Hausdorffness recur: definitions, lower-limit examples, compact subsets of Hausdorff spaces being closed, and compact-Hausdorff arguments involving the Cantor set.

Connectedness is consistently examinable: definitions, separations in discrete/indiscrete/subspace/cofinite examples, continuous images, the IVT link and using connectedness to rule out homeomorphisms.
Homeomorphism and homotopy remain highly likely. The 2025-2026 paper asks for three homeomorphism comparisons and an explicit linear homotopy between arbitrary maps R^n -> R^n .
Euler characteristic, triangulation, Brouwer/fundamental-theorem applications and Nash-style questions are older-pattern topics; keep them as secondary revision.
details.name: Topology

families.title: Topology Definitions, Standard Examples, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
appearances: 2023/24 - Q1(a) - define a topology and give two distinct topologies on a finite set. [5 marks]
2023/24 - Q1(b) - define a subspace topology and show the usual subspace topology on Q is not discrete. [5 marks]
2023/24 - Q1(c) - define a basis and give the lower-limit basis. [5 marks]
2023/24 - Q1(d)-(e) - define closure, prove the neighbourhood characterisation, and find the closure of (0,1) in the lower-limit topology. [10 marks]
2024/25 - Q1(a) - repeat topology definition plus two finite topologies. [5 marks]
2024/25 - Q1(b)-(d) - compare cofinite and discrete topologies on Z; show Z is discrete as a subspace of R; give the lower-limit basis and show [0,1) is clopen. [15 marks]
2024/25 - Q1(e) - define neighbourhood and interior, then prove the neighbourhood/interior equivalence. [5 marks]

2025/26 - Q1(a)-(e) - define topology, standard and cofinite topologies, closure, interior and subspace topology; decide whether [0,1] is discrete; prove no accumulation points implies closed. [25 marks]
families.question: Let X be a set or topological space. State the exact definition requested, then work with a named topology or subspace: compare two topologies, give a basis, decide whether a subspace is discrete, or prove a closure/interior/accumulation-point claim by neighbourhoods.
families.answer: Reusable answer: A topology τ on X contains ∅ and X, is closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. For subspaces, write opens as A∩U where U is open in the ambient space. For the lower-limit topology use the basis {[a,b):a<b}; for cofinite spaces use ∅ and sets with finite complement. When deciding if a subspace is discrete, test a singleton: an interior point such as 1/2 in [0,1] cannot be relatively open, but Z is discrete in R because each n is isolated by a small interval. For closure use “every neighbourhood meets A”; for accumulation points use “every neighbourhood meets A\{x}”. To prove a set closed from no accumulation points, show every x outside it has an open neighbourhood disjoint from it.

families.title: Compactness, Hausdorffness, Cofinite And Lower-Limit Examples
appearances: 2023/24 - Q2(a)-(b) - define compactness and decide whether standard R is compact. [9 marks]
2023/24 - Q3(a) - decide whether cofinite R is compact and Hausdorff. [6 marks]
2023/24 - Q3(c) - show a continuous bijection between compact Hausdorff spaces is a homeomorphism. [5 marks]
2024/25 - Q2(a)-(e) - dense subsets of cofinite R; compactness; closed subsets of compact spaces; non-compactness of lower-limit R; and Hausdorff comparisons for cofinite Z and standard R. [25 marks]

2025/26 - Q2(b)-(e) - cofinite density; define compactness and disprove compactness of lower-limit R; define and prove lower-limit Hausdorffness; prove a compact subspace of a Hausdorff space is closed. [22 marks]
families.question: For a standard, cofinite, or lower-limit topology, state compactness or Hausdorffness exactly, decide the property using a topology-valid cover or separation, then prove the associated compactness theorem under its stated hypotheses.
families.answer: Reusable answer: Compact means every open cover has a finite subcover. To disprove compactness of the lower-limit line, use the basic-open cover {[n,n+1):n∈Z}; every finite subfamily is bounded. A cofinite topology on an infinite set is compact but not Hausdorff: every open cover has a finite subcover, while two nonempty cofinite opens must intersect. For lower-limit R, if x<y then [x,y) and [y,y+1) are disjoint basic neighbourhoods, so it is Hausdorff. For a compact A in Hausdorff X, separate x∉A from each a∈A, use compactness to select finitely many neighbourhoods of points of A, and intersect the corresponding finitely many neighbourhoods of x to show X\A is open.

families.title: Connectedness, Separations, Continuous Images, And IVT
appearances: 2023/24 - Q3(b) - prove a continuous surjective image of a connected space is connected and derive IVT. [8 marks]
2024/25 - Q3(b) - define connectedness and give connected/disconnected examples. [8 marks]
2024/25 - Q4(a) - repeat the continuous-surjection proof and IVT consequence. [6 marks]
2025/26 - Q3(b)-(c) - define connectedness; classify Q with discrete, indiscrete, usual subspace and cofinite topologies, giving separations where required. [13 marks]
2025/26 - Q4(b) - repeat the continuous-surjection proof and IVT consequence. [6 marks]
families.question: Define connectedness. Given an explicit topology, either exhibit a separation or rule one out; then prove that a continuous surjection preserves connectedness and explain its Intermediate Value Theorem consequence.
families.answer: Reusable answer: A separation of X is X=U∪V where U and V are disjoint, nonempty, open subsets of X. A space is connected when no separation exists. If f:X→Y is continuous and onto and Y=U∪V were a separation, f -1 (U) and f -1 (V) would be a separation of X; continuity gives openness and surjectivity gives nonemptiness and coverage. For IVT, [a,b] is connected, so h([a,b]) is a connected subset of R and hence an interval containing h(a) and h(b).

families.title: Homeomorphism Comparisons And Invariants
appearances: 2023/24 - Q2(c) - compare [0,1], (0,1), S 1 , and R\{0}; justify all six non-homeomorphism comparisons. [12 marks]
2024/25 - Q3(c) - show R and [0,1] are not homeomorphic, R 2 and R are not homeomorphic, and R and (0,∞) are homeomorphic. [9 marks]
2025/26 - Q3(d) - show S 1 and [0,1] are not homeomorphic, R and [0,1] are not homeomorphic, and R and (0,∞) are homeomorphic. [9 marks]
families.question: For each listed pair of spaces, choose the cheapest topological invariant that distinguishes them, or construct an explicit continuous bijection with continuous inverse.
families.answer: Reusable answer: Homeomorphisms preserve compactness and connectedness, including connectedness after deleting corresponding points. [0,1] is compact and R is not, so they are not homeomorphic. S 1 and [0,1] are both compact and connected, so use point removal: delete the preimage of 1/2 under a hypothetical homeomorphism. The punctured circle remains connected, whereas [0,1]\{1/2} is disconnected. For a positive result, f(x)=e x is a homeomorphism R→(0,∞), with inverse ln.

families.title: Product, Initial/Final, And Quotient Topologies
appearances: 2023/24 - Q2(d) - write down a base for the product topology on X×Y. [4 marks]
2023/24 - Q4(a)-(b) - define the quotient topology on X/~ and show S 1 is a quotient of [0,1]. [9 marks]
2024/25 - Q3(a) - define the initial topology induced by a family of functions. [4 marks]
2024/25 - Q4(b)-(d) - repeat the product basis, quotient topology, and S 1 as a quotient of [0,1]. [13 marks]
2025/26 - Q3(a) - define the final topology with respect to a family of functions. [3 marks]
2025/26 - Q4(c)-(d) - explain why S 1 is a quotient of [0,1], then decide whether R is a quotient of the Cantor set. [8 marks]
families.question: State the construction precisely: basis rectangles for products, pullbacks for initial/final topologies, or the quotient-open-set rule. Then apply it to a quotient map, especially the endpoint identification [0,1]/(0~1), or use a preserved property to rule a quotient out.
families.answer: Reusable answer: A product basis consists of U×V with U and V open. The initial topology is the coarsest topology making the given maps out of a set continuous; the final topology is the finest topology making the given maps into a set continuous. A quotient topology on X/~ declares W open exactly when q -1 (W) is open in X. For S 1 , use q(t)=e 2πit : it is a continuous surjection and identifies exactly 0 and 1. R cannot be a quotient of compact Cantor C because a quotient map would be a continuous surjection C→R, forcing R to be compact.

families.title: Cantor Set: Definition, Images, Compactness, And Quotients
appearances: 2023/24 - Q3(d) - show [0,1] is a continuous image of C, then decide whether C is a continuous image of [0,1]. [6 marks]
2024/25 - Q3(d) - define the Cantor set. [4 marks]
2025/26 - Q4(a) - define C and explain why it is compact Hausdorff. [5 marks]
2025/26 - Q4(d) - decide whether standard R is a quotient of C. [3 marks]
families.question: Define the Cantor set, state its compact-Hausdorff properties, and reason carefully about what can be its continuous image or quotient using compactness, connectedness, and an explicit map where supplied.
families.answer: Reusable answer: Define C by repeatedly removing the open middle third from each remaining closed interval, equivalently as the points of [0,1] with a ternary expansion using only 0 and 2. It is compact because it is closed in compact [0,1], and Hausdorff because it is a subspace of R. Use compactness under continuous images to rule out a continuous surjection or quotient from C onto non-compact R. Do not reverse image claims automatically: [0,1] is a continuous image of C, but connectedness blocks a continuous surjection [0,1]→C because C is disconnected.

families.title: Homotopy, Homotopy Equivalence, And Convex/Star-Shaped Spaces
appearances: 2023/24 - Q4(c)-(e) - define homotopy and homotopy equivalence, define simply connected, and show every star-shaped subset of R n is simply connected. [16 marks]
2024/25 - Q4(e) - define homotopy and show continuous f,g:R m →R n are homotopic. [6 marks]
2025/26 - Q4(e) - repeat the homotopy definition and show continuous f,g:R n →R n are homotopic. [6 marks]
families.question: Define homotopy with its full domain, codomain, continuity and endpoint conditions. Then construct a homotopy by straight-line interpolation in a convex target, or a contraction in a star-shaped space.
families.answer: Reusable answer: Maps f,g:X→Y are homotopic if a continuous H:X×[0,1]→Y exists with H(x,0)=f(x) and H(x,1)=g(x). For maps into R n , take H(x,t)=(1−t)f(x)+tg(x). It is continuous and remains in R n . More generally this works for any convex target. For a star-shaped set with centre x 0 , H(x,t)=(1−t)x+tx 0 contracts the space, provided the entire line segment stays inside it.

families.title: Other Distinct Older Question Shapes
appearances: Topology-axiom validation and components: test proposed open-set families, exhibit a failed axiom if necessary, and find connected components if valid. Appears in 2018/19 Q4, 2021/22 Q4, and 2022/23 Q3.

Cofinite-space continuity: decide connectedness/compactness and give continuous or non-continuous self-maps of a cofinite space. Appears in 2018/19 Q5 and 2021/22 Q5; it complements the current cofinite compactness/Hausdorff family.
Homotopy-equivalence variants: show S 1 is homotopy equivalent to C\{0}, or classify plane letters by homeomorphism/homotopy type. Appears in 2018/19 Q8, 2021/22 Q7, and 2022/23 Q8.
Graph/dendrogram application: construct threshold graphs and a dendrogram from a distance table. Appears only in 2022/23 Q6.
Older homeomorphism pair: decide whether Z and Q are homeomorphic in their usual subspace topologies. Appears only in 2021/22 Q6.

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: Define a topology on X.
cards.back: A collection τ of subsets of X such that ∅ and X belong to τ, arbitrary unions of members of τ belong to τ, and finite intersections of members of τ belong to τ.

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: What is the standard topology on R?
cards.back: The topology whose open sets are arbitrary unions of ordinary open intervals (a,b).

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: What is the cofinite topology on X?
cards.back: The topology whose open sets are ∅ together with all subsets U⊆X for which X\U is finite.

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: What is the discrete topology on X?
cards.back: The topology P(X), in which every subset of X is open.

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: How can you show the standard and cofinite topologies on R are different?
cards.back: The interval (0,1) is open in the standard topology. Its complement R\(0,1) is infinite, so (0,1) is not open in the cofinite topology. Therefore the two topologies differ.

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: What is the subspace topology on A⊆X?
cards.back: The open sets of A are precisely the sets A∩U, where U is open in X. Thus V⊆A is open in A if and only if V=A∩U for some open U⊆X.

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: When is a subspace discrete?
cards.back: A subspace A is discrete if and only if every singleton {a}, with a∈A, is open in the subspace topology. Equivalently, every subset of A is open.

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: Why is Q not discrete in its usual subspace topology?
cards.back: Every ordinary open interval containing q∈Q contains another rational. Therefore no interval intersects Q in {q}, so {q} is not open in Q.

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: Why is Z discrete in its usual subspace topology?
cards.back: For every n∈Z, (n−1/2,n+1/2)∩Z={n}. Thus every singleton of Z is open, so Z is discrete.

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: Why is [0,1] not discrete in its usual subspace topology?
cards.back: Every ordinary open interval containing 1/2 meets [0,1] in points other than 1/2. Thus {1/2} is not open in [0,1], so [0,1] is not discrete.

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: What is a basis, and what is the lower-limit basis on R?
cards.back: A basis B is a collection of open sets such that every open set is a union of members of B. For the lower-limit topology on R, B={[a,b): a,b∈R and a<b}.

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: What does clopen mean, and why is [0,1) clopen in the lower-limit topology?
cards.back: Clopen means both open and closed. [0,1) is a basic open set. Its complement is (−∞,0)∪[1,∞)=⋃ n≥1 [−n,0)∪⋃ n≥1 [1,n+1), so it is open; hence [0,1) is closed as well.

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: What is a neighbourhood, and how does it characterise interior?
cards.back: A neighbourhood of a point is any set that contains an open set around that point. The interior of a set consists of the points that have an open neighbourhood lying completely inside the set.

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: What is the closure of A?
cards.back: The closure of A is A together with every point that cannot be separated from A by an open neighbourhood.

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: What is an accumulation point of A?
cards.back: A point where every neighbourhood contains points of A other than possibly the point itself.

cards.group: Core Topology, Subspaces, Bases, Closure, And Interior
cards.front: Why does having no accumulation points imply that A is closed?
cards.back: Every point outside A has an open neighbourhood that does not meet A. Therefore the complement of A is open, so A is closed.

cards.group: Compactness, Hausdorffness, Cofinite, And Lower-Limit Examples
cards.front: What does compact mean?
cards.back: A space is compact if, whenever it is covered by open sets, finitely many of those open sets already cover the whole space.

cards.group: Compactness, Hausdorffness, Cofinite, And Lower-Limit Examples
cards.front: Is standard R compact?
cards.back: No. The intervals (−n,n) cover all real numbers, but any finite selection misses sufficiently large positive and negative numbers.

cards.group: Compactness, Hausdorffness, Cofinite, And Lower-Limit Examples
cards.front: How can you disprove compactness of the lower-limit line?
cards.back: The intervals [n,n+1), for integers n, cover the whole line. Any finite selection covers only a bounded part of the line, so it cannot cover everything.

cards.group: Compactness, Hausdorffness, Cofinite, And Lower-Limit Examples
cards.front: What does dense mean, and which sets are dense in a cofinite space?
cards.back: A set is dense if every nonempty open set meets it. In an infinite cofinite space, every infinite subset is dense, because a nonempty open set leaves out only finitely many points.

cards.group: Compactness, Hausdorffness, Cofinite, And Lower-Limit Examples
cards.front: Is an infinite cofinite space compact?
cards.back: Yes. Choose one nonempty set from an open cover; it misses only finitely many points. Choose one cover set for each missed point, giving a finite subcover.

cards.group: Compactness, Hausdorffness, Cofinite, And Lower-Limit Examples
cards.front: Why is an infinite cofinite space not Hausdorff?
cards.back: Any two nonempty open sets must overlap, because each leaves out only finitely many points. Therefore two different points cannot always be placed in disjoint open neighbourhoods.

cards.group: Compactness, Hausdorffness, Cofinite, And Lower-Limit Examples
cards.front: What does Hausdorff mean?
cards.back: A space is Hausdorff if any two different points can be placed in disjoint open neighbourhoods.

cards.group: Compactness, Hausdorffness, Cofinite, And Lower-Limit Examples
cards.front: Why is the lower-limit topology on R Hausdorff?
cards.back: If x<y, the open intervals [x,y) and [y,y+1) contain x and y respectively and do not overlap. Thus any two different points can be separated by disjoint open neighbourhoods.

cards.group: Compactness, Hausdorffness, Cofinite, And Lower-Limit Examples
cards.front: Why is every closed subset of a compact space compact?
cards.back: Start with an open cover of the closed subset. Add its open complement to cover the whole space. Compactness gives a finite cover, and removing the complement leaves a finite cover of the subset. Therefore the subset is compact.

cards.group: Compactness, Hausdorffness, Cofinite, And Lower-Limit Examples
cards.front: Why is a compact subspace of a Hausdorff space closed?
cards.back: Take a point outside the compact set. Separate it from each point of the compact set using disjoint open neighbourhoods. Compactness reduces these to finitely many; intersect the neighbourhoods around the outside point to get an open neighbourhood missing the compact set. Therefore the complement is open, so the compact set is closed.

cards.group: Compactness, Hausdorffness, Cofinite, And Lower-Limit Examples
cards.front: Why is a continuous bijection from compact X to Hausdorff Y a homeomorphism?
cards.back: A closed subset of compact X is compact. Its image is compact, and compact subsets of Hausdorff Y are closed. So the map sends closed sets to closed sets, which makes its inverse continuous. Therefore it is a homeomorphism.

cards.group: Connectedness, Separations, Continuous Images, And IVT
cards.front: What is a separation of X?
cards.back: A pair U,V of disjoint, nonempty, open subsets of X whose union is X: X=U∪V.

cards.group: Connectedness, Separations, Continuous Images, And IVT
cards.front: What does connected mean?
cards.back: A space is connected if it has no separation; equivalently, its only clopen subsets are ∅ and X.

cards.group: Connectedness, Separations, Continuous Images, And IVT
cards.front: Why is discrete Q disconnected?
cards.back: {0} and Q\{0} are disjoint, nonempty, open sets whose union is Q.

cards.group: Connectedness, Separations, Continuous Images, And IVT
cards.front: Why is indiscrete Q connected?
cards.back: The only open sets are ∅ and Q, so there is no nonempty proper open set that could form a separation.

cards.group: Connectedness, Separations, Continuous Images, And IVT
cards.front: Why is Q with the usual subspace topology disconnected?
cards.back: Let U=Q∩(−∞,√2) and V=Q∩(√2,∞). They are nonempty, disjoint, relatively open in Q, and U∪V=Q because √2∉Q. Hence they form a separation.

cards.group: Connectedness, Separations, Continuous Images, And IVT
cards.front: Why is cofinite Q connected?
cards.back: Every two nonempty cofinite open subsets of the infinite set Q intersect. A separation would require two disjoint nonempty open sets, so no separation exists.

cards.group: Connectedness, Separations, Continuous Images, And IVT
cards.front: Why is a continuous surjective image of a connected space connected?
cards.back: Let f:X→Y be continuous and surjective, with X connected. If Y=U∪V were a separation, then f −1 (U) and f −1 (V) would be disjoint, nonempty, open sets covering X—a contradiction. Hence Y is connected.

cards.group: Connectedness, Separations, Continuous Images, And IVT
cards.front: How does connectedness give the Intermediate Value Theorem?
cards.back: For continuous h:[a,b]→R, the interval [a,b] is connected, so h([a,b]) is connected and therefore an interval. Every value t between h(a) and h(b) lies in h([a,b]), so h(c)=t for some c∈[a,b].

cards.group: Homeomorphisms And Invariants
cards.front: What is a homeomorphism?
cards.back: A bijection f:X→Y such that both f and f −1 :Y→X are continuous. It is an isomorphism of topological spaces.

cards.group: Homeomorphisms And Invariants
cards.front: What properties are used as homeomorphism invariants in these papers?
cards.back: Compactness and connectedness, including connectedness after deleting corresponding points.

cards.group: Homeomorphisms And Invariants
cards.front: Why are R and [0,1] not homeomorphic?
cards.back: [0,1] is compact and R is not, and compactness is preserved by homeomorphisms.

cards.group: Homeomorphisms And Invariants
cards.front: Why are R 2 and R not homeomorphic?
cards.back: If h:R→R 2 were a homeomorphism, then h would restrict to a homeomorphism R\{0}→R 2 \{h(0)}. But R\{0} is disconnected, whereas R 2 \{h(0)} is path-connected. This contradiction proves they are not homeomorphic.

cards.group: Homeomorphisms And Invariants
cards.front: Why are S 1 and [0,1] not homeomorphic, and when is point removal useful?
cards.back: If h:[0,1]→S 1 were a homeomorphism, remove an interior point 1/2 and its image h(1/2). The space [0,1]\{1/2} is disconnected, whereas S 1 \{h(1/2)} is connected. This contradiction shows they are not homeomorphic. Point removal is useful when simpler invariants agree but punctured spaces have different connectedness.

cards.group: Homeomorphisms And Invariants
cards.front: Give a homeomorphism R→(0,∞) and its inverse.
cards.back: f(x)=e x is a continuous bijection from R to (0,∞), and f −1 (y)=ln(y) is continuous. Therefore f is a homeomorphism.

cards.group: Product, Initial, Final, And Quotient Topologies
cards.front: What is a basis for the product topology on X×Y?
cards.back: The sets U×V, where U is open in X and V is open in Y, form a basis. The product-open sets are arbitrary unions of these rectangles.

cards.group: Product, Initial, Final, And Quotient Topologies
cards.front: Define the initial and final topologies.
cards.back: For maps f i :X→Y i , the initial topology on X is the coarsest topology making every f i continuous; it is generated by f i −1 (U) for U open in Y i . For maps g i :X i →Y, the final topology on Y is the finest topology making every g i continuous; W⊆Y is open exactly when every g i −1 (W) is open in X i .

cards.group: Product, Initial, Final, And Quotient Topologies
cards.front: What is the quotient topology on X/~?
cards.back: Let q:X→X/~ send x to its equivalence class [x]. The quotient topology is the final topology for q: a set W⊆X/~ is open if and only if q −1 (W) is open in X.

cards.group: Product, Initial, Final, And Quotient Topologies
cards.front: Why is S 1 a quotient of [0,1], and how is the identification written?
cards.back: The map q(t)=(cos(2πt),sin(2πt)) is a continuous surjection [0,1]→S 1 . It identifies exactly 0 and 1, so it induces a continuous bijection [0,1]/(0~1)→S 1 . The quotient is compact and S 1 is Hausdorff, so this bijection is a homeomorphism. Thus S 1 ≅[0,1]/(0~1).

cards.group: Cantor Set: Definition, Compactness, Images, And Quotients
cards.front: How is the Cantor set C constructed?
cards.back: Start with C 0 =[0,1]. At each stage remove the open middle third of every closed interval remaining from the previous stage. The Cantor set is C=⋂ n≥0 C n .

cards.group: Cantor Set: Definition, Compactness, Images, And Quotients
cards.front: How can the Cantor set be described using ternary expansions?
cards.back: C is the set of points in [0,1] having a ternary expansion that uses only the digits 0 and 2. Equivalently, its points are ∑ n=1 ∞ 2a n /3 n , where each a n is 0 or 1.

cards.group: Cantor Set: Definition, Compactness, Images, And Quotients
cards.front: Why is the Cantor set compact Hausdorff?
cards.back: Each C n is closed in [0,1], so C=⋂C n is closed in compact [0,1]; hence C is compact. As a subspace of the Hausdorff space R, C is Hausdorff.

cards.group: Cantor Set: Definition, Compactness, Images, And Quotients
cards.front: Which continuous-image directions hold between C and [0,1]?
cards.back: [0,1] is a continuous image of C: the restriction of the Cantor function sends ∑ n=1 ∞ 2a n /3 n to ∑ n=1 ∞ a n /2 n and is surjective. Conversely, C cannot be a continuous image of [0,1], because a continuous image of connected [0,1] is connected, while C is disconnected.

cards.group: Cantor Set: Definition, Compactness, Images, And Quotients
cards.front: What property rules out a quotient map from C onto standard R?
cards.back: A quotient map is a continuous surjection. Since C is compact, its continuous image would be compact; standard R is not compact. Therefore R cannot be a quotient of C.

cards.group: Homotopy And Star-Shaped/Convex Spaces
cards.front: When are f,g:X→Y homotopic?
cards.back: They are homotopic if there is a continuous H:X×[0,1]→Y such that H(x,0)=f(x) and H(x,1)=g(x) for every x∈X. H is a homotopy from f to g.

cards.group: Homotopy And Star-Shaped/Convex Spaces
cards.front: When are X and Y homotopy equivalent?
cards.back: When there are continuous maps f:X→Y and g:Y→X such that g∘f is homotopic to id X and f∘g is homotopic to id Y .

cards.group: Homotopy And Star-Shaped/Convex Spaces
cards.front: What does simply connected mean?
cards.back: A space X is simply connected if it is path-connected and every loop in X is homotopic, while fixing its endpoints, to a constant loop. Equivalently, its fundamental group is trivial.

cards.group: Homotopy And Star-Shaped/Convex Spaces
cards.front: What straight-line homotopy works for maps into R n , and why?
cards.back: For continuous f,g:X→R n , set H(x,t)=(1−t)f(x)+tg(x). This is continuous, has H(x,0)=f(x) and H(x,1)=g(x), and stays in R n ; hence it is a homotopy.

cards.group: Homotopy And Star-Shaped/Convex Spaces
cards.front: For what more general targets does straight-line interpolation work?
cards.back: It works for a convex subset Y⊆R n : whenever y 0 ,y 1 ∈Y and t∈[0,1], (1−t)y 0 +ty 1 lies in Y. Thus the same formula gives a homotopy between maps into Y.

cards.group: Homotopy And Star-Shaped/Convex Spaces
cards.front: How do you contract a star-shaped space with centre x 0 ?
cards.back: S is star-shaped with centre x 0 if, for every x∈S, the segment {(1−t)x+tx 0 :t∈[0,1]} lies in S. Then H(x,t)=(1−t)x+tx 0 contracts S to x 0 ; hence S is contractible and therefore simply connected.

sheets.title: Compactness
sheets.purpose: State compactness exactly, disprove it with a topology-valid cover, and combine it with Hausdorff separation. Exam use: In 2025/26, Q2(d) asks for the definition and non-compactness of the lower-limit line for 5 marks, while Q2(e) asks for the compact-subspace-of-Hausdorff closedness proof for 5 marks.

practice.title: Medium/hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: The lower-limit real line R ℓ is not compact. The basic-open sets U n =[n,n+1), n∈Z, cover R. Any finite subfamily covers only a bounded union of these intervals and therefore misses all sufficiently large positive and negative real numbers. Hence this open cover has no finite subcover.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridges
practice.prompt: 1. Foundation: Why is the Cantor set compact Hausdorff? Check: it is closed in compact [0,1], and it inherits Hausdorffness from R.
practice.route: 2. Exam style: Prove a closed F⊆X is compact when X is compact. Check: add X\F to an arbitrary cover of F.
practice.answer: 2. Exam style: Prove a closed F⊆X is compact when X is compact. Check: add X\F to an arbitrary cover of F.

practice.title: Hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: If X is compact, Y Hausdorff and f:X→Y continuous and bijective, then f is a homeomorphism. For closed F⊆X, F is compact, so f(F) is compact and therefore closed in Hausdorff Y. Thus f is closed, which makes f -1 continuous.

practice.title: Practice question - lower-limit and Hausdorff compactness [10 marks]
practice.prompt: (a) Define compactness and decide, with justification, whether the lower-limit real line R ℓ is compact. [5 marks] (b) Let A be a compact subspace of a Hausdorff space X. Show that A is closed in X. [5 marks]
practice.route: an infinite intersection of the V a need not be open; compactness is what reduces it to a finite intersection.
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: use the integer-indexed half-open cover for (a); for (b), separate a fixed x∉A from each a∈A and use compactness to retain only finitely many separating neighbourhoods.

mistakes: Choosing a finite cover instead of proving a finite subcover of an arbitrary cover.
Using Heine–Borel outside Euclidean space.
Forgetting closedness in the closed-subset theorem.
Recovery rule: A sequence argument is not automatically available in an arbitrary topological space; use open covers unless sequential compactness has been established.

sheets.title: Connectedness
sheets.purpose: Classify spaces by constructing or ruling out separations, then transfer connectedness through continuous surjections. Exam use: The 2025/26 paper devotes 13 marks in Q3(b-c) to the definition and four topologies on Q, then 6 marks in Q4(b) to continuous images and the Intermediate Value Theorem.

practice.title: Medium/hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: On Q, connectedness depends on the topology. The discrete topology is disconnected via {0} and Q\{0}. The indiscrete topology is connected because it has no nonempty proper open set. The usual subspace topology is disconnected via Q∩(-∞,√2) and Q∩(√2,∞). The cofinite topology is connected because Q is infinite and any two nonempty cofinite-open sets intersect.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridges
practice.prompt: 1. Foundation [3 marks]: Define connectedness using separations. Check: include open, disjoint, nonempty and covering.
practice.route: 2. Exam style [6 marks]: If f:X→Y is continuous and onto and X connected, prove Y connected, then explain the IVT consequence. Check: pull back a separation, then use that a connected subset of R is an interval.
practice.answer: 2. Exam style [6 marks]: If f:X→Y is continuous and onto and X connected, prove Y connected, then explain the IVT consequence. Check: pull back a separation, then use that a connected subset of R is an interval.

practice.title: Hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Let h:[a,b]→R be continuous and suppose h(a)≤y≤h(b). The interval [a,b] is connected, so h([a,b]) is connected by the continuous-image theorem. Connected subsets of R are intervals. Since h([a,b]) contains h(a) and h(b), it contains every value between them, in particular y. Thus h(c)=y for some c∈[a,b], which is the Intermediate Value Theorem.

practice.title: Practice question - four topologies on Q [13 marks]
practice.prompt: (a) Define connectedness. [3 marks] (b) Decide whether Q is connected with each of the discrete, indiscrete, usual subspace and cofinite topologies. Exhibit a separation for every disconnected case and briefly justify every connected case. [10 marks]
practice.route: the rational cut must occur at an irrational number; cutting at a rational leaves that point uncovered unless the sets are changed.
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: use a singleton for the discrete case, the absence of proper opens for the indiscrete case, an irrational cut for the usual subspace case, and unavoidable intersections for the infinite cofinite case.

mistakes: Forgetting the sets in a separation must be nonempty.
Using images rather than preimages in the theorem proof.
Assuming every connected space is path connected.
Recovery rule: The separating sets need only be open in the subspace under discussion, not necessarily open in the ambient space.

sheets.title: Continuity and Homeomorphism
sheets.purpose: Test continuity through preimages and rule in or out homeomorphisms using the cheapest valid invariant. Exam use: The 2025/26 Q3(d) groups three homeomorphism decisions into 9 marks: one point-removal argument, one compactness obstruction and one explicit positive construction.

practice.title: Medium/hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: The three 2025/26 comparisons use different fastest routes. S 1 is not homeomorphic to [0,1]: if h existed, delete h -1 (1/2); the punctured circle is connected but [0,1]\{1/2} is disconnected. Standard R is not homeomorphic to [0,1] because the interval is compact and R is not. Finally, x↦e x is a homeomorphism R→(0,∞), with continuous inverse ln.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridges
practice.prompt: 1. Foundation: Why does compactness rule out a homeomorphism R→[0,1]? Check: compactness is preserved, [0,1] is compact and R is not.
practice.route: 2. Exam style: Show [0,1] is not homeomorphic to S¹. Check: remove an interior point of the interval and the corresponding point of the circle, then compare connectedness.
practice.answer: 2. Exam style: Show [0,1] is not homeomorphic to S¹. Check: remove an interior point of the interval and the corresponding point of the circle, then compare connectedness.

practice.title: Hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: To use point removal rigorously, suppose h:S 1 →[0,1] is a homeomorphism and let p=h -1 (1/2). The restriction h| S¹\{p} is a homeomorphism onto [0,1]\{1/2}. But S 1 \{p} is homeomorphic to an open interval and is connected, whereas [0,1]\{1/2} is separated by [0,1/2) and (1/2,1]. Contradiction.

practice.title: Practice question - three homeomorphism decisions [9 marks]
practice.prompt: (a) Show S 1 and [0,1] are not homeomorphic. (b) Show R and [0,1] are not homeomorphic. (c) Show R and (0,∞) are homeomorphic. [9 marks]
practice.route: connectedness alone does not distinguish S 1 from [0,1]; the distinguishing invariant is connectedness after deleting corresponding points.
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: use point-removal connectedness for (a), compactness for (b), and the exponential/logarithm pair for (c).

mistakes: Testing images of opens instead of preimages.
Calling a continuous bijection a homeomorphism without an inverse argument.
Using an invariant that is not actually topological.
Recovery rule: A continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism; verify inverse continuity or cite a theorem that supplies it.

sheets.title: Hausdorff Spaces
sheets.purpose: Test whether distinct points can be separated by disjoint open sets and exploit compact-Hausdorff consequences. Exam use: In 2025/26, Q2(c) assigns 6 marks to the definition and the lower-limit line, Q2(e) uses Hausdorffness in a 5-mark closedness proof, and Q4(a) asks why the Cantor set is compact Hausdorff.

practice.title: Medium/hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: The lower-limit real line R ℓ is Hausdorff. Given x<y, take U=[x,y) and V=[y,y+1). Both are basic open sets, x∈U, y∈V, and U∩V=∅. Reversing the labels handles y<x, so every pair of distinct points has disjoint open neighbourhoods.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridges
practice.prompt: 1. Foundation: Is an infinite cofinite space Hausdorff? Check: no: two nonempty opens always intersect, even though every singleton is closed.
practice.route: 2. Exam style [5 marks]: Prove a compact subspace A of Hausdorff X is closed. Check: separate each x∉A from all of A using a finite subcover.
practice.answer: 2. Exam style [5 marks]: Prove a compact subspace A of Hausdorff X is closed. Check: separate each x∉A from all of A using a finite subcover.

practice.title: Hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: The Cantor set C is Hausdorff because it is a subspace of standard R, and subspaces of Hausdorff spaces are Hausdorff. It is compact because it is closed in the compact interval [0,1]. Both claims require naming the inherited topology and the relevant hereditary theorem.

practice.title: Practice question - lower-limit Hausdorffness [6 marks]
practice.prompt: (a) Define what it means for a topological space to be Hausdorff. (b) Decide, with justification, whether the real line with the lower-limit topology is Hausdorff. [6 marks]
practice.route: [x,y) and [y,y+1) work because the first interval excludes y; ordinary closed intervals would not be open in the lower-limit topology.
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: order arbitrary distinct points and use adjacent half-open basis intervals whose shared endpoint belongs only to the second interval.

mistakes: Finding neighbourhoods that are not disjoint.
Assuming T₁ automatically means Hausdorff.
Omitting continuity in the compact-Hausdorff theorem.
Recovery rule: T1 separates a point from another by one open set; it does not provide the pair of disjoint neighbourhoods required for Hausdorffness.

sheets.title: Homotopy and Simply Connected Spaces
sheets.purpose: State a homotopy precisely and exploit convex codomains to construct it by linear interpolation; keep contractions and simple connectedness as related secondary material. Exam use: The 2025/26 Q4(e) allocates 6 marks to the definition and to proving that arbitrary continuous maps R n →R n are homotopic.

practice.title: Medium/hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Let f,g:R n →R n be continuous. Define H(x,t)=(1−t)f(x)+tg(x). Then H(x,0)=f(x) and H(x,1)=g(x). The formula is continuous as a combination of continuous maps, and every value is in R n . Hence f and g are homotopic.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridges
practice.prompt: 1. Foundation: Show any two constant maps X→R are homotopic. Check: linearly interpolate their values and verify both endpoints.
practice.route: 2. Exam style: Generalise the paper argument to maps f,g:X→C where C⊆R n is convex. Check: the segment between f(x) and g(x) remains in C.
practice.answer: 2. Exam style: Generalise the paper argument to maps f,g:X→C where C⊆R n is convex. Check: the segment between f(x) and g(x) remains in C.

practice.title: Hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Convexity is sufficient but not necessary for two maps to be homotopic. The straight-line formula can fail for a non-convex codomain: interpolating two points of S 1 generally passes through the disk rather than staying on the circle. A valid formula must land in the declared codomain for every (x,t).

practice.title: Practice question - arbitrary maps into R n [6 marks]
practice.prompt: (a) Define what it means for continuous maps f,g:X→Y to be homotopic. (b) Let f,g:R n →R n be continuous. Show that f and g are homotopic. [6 marks]
practice.route: do not use H(x,t)=(1−t)x unless f is the identity and g is the zero map; the paper asks about arbitrary f and g.
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: give the complete definition, then use straight-line interpolation in the convex codomain R n .

mistakes: Giving a family H without endpoint checks.
Failing to prove H takes values in the target space.
Calling a connected space simply connected without addressing loops.
Recovery rule: A formula that leaves the space is not a homotopy in that space; verify the codomain condition for every t.

sheets.title: Neighbourhoods, Interior, Closure and Density
sheets.purpose: Define and compute interior and closure, use accumulation points correctly, and prove density via neighbourhood intersections. Exam use: In 2025/26 these ideas occur in three different parts: definitions in Q1(c), a 5-mark closedness proof in Q1(e), and a 6-mark cofinite-density example in Q2(b).

practice.title: Medium/hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Let A be a subset of a topological space X with no accumulation point in X. For x∈X\A, x is not an accumulation point, so some open neighbourhood U of x satisfies U∩(A\{x})=∅. Since x∉A, this simplifies to U∩A=∅. Thus every point of X\A has an open neighbourhood contained in X\A, so X\A is open and A is closed.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridges
practice.prompt: 1. Foundation: Find cl({1/n:n≥1}) in R. Check: include 0.
practice.route: 2. Exam style [6 marks]: In the cofinite topology on Z, give a proper dense subset. Check: take 2Z; it is proper and infinite, and every nonempty cofinite-open set meets every infinite subset.
practice.answer: 2. Exam style [6 marks]: In the cofinite topology on Z, give a proper dense subset. Check: take 2Z; it is proper and infinite, and every nonempty cofinite-open set meets every infinite subset.

practice.title: Hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Paper-style synthesis: in the subspace X=[0,1], find interior and closure of A=[0,1/2). Check int_X A=[0,1/2), since [0,epsilon)=X intersect (-1,epsilon) is open in X; cl_X A=[0,1/2]. This differs from ambient interior in R.
practice.route: in the subspace X=[0,1], find interior and closure of A=[0,1/2). Check int_X A=[0,1/2), since [0,epsilon)=X intersect (-1,epsilon) is open in X; cl_X A=[0,1/2]. This differs from ambient interior in R.
practice.answer: in the subspace X=[0,1], find interior and closure of A=[0,1/2). Check int_X A=[0,1/2), since [0,epsilon)=X intersect (-1,epsilon) is open in X; cl_X A=[0,1/2]. This differs from ambient interior in R.

practice.title: Practice question - no accumulation points [5 marks]
practice.prompt: Let A be a subset of a topological space X. Show that if A has no accumulation point in X, then A is closed in X. [5 marks]
practice.route: the definition removes {x}; explicitly use x∉A before replacing A\{x} by A.
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: prove X\A open point-by-point; restricting to x∉A turns a neighbourhood avoiding A\{x} into one avoiding all of A.

mistakes: Treating closure as A plus only “visible” endpoints.
Using metric-ball intuition without checking the topology.
For density, checking only one neighbourhood.
Recovery rule: Endpoints can be interior points in a subspace; always name the ambient space before computing.

sheets.title: Secondary Applications
sheets.purpose: Prepare the Intermediate Value Theorem as a current connectedness application, while retaining Euler/triangulation, Brouwer, FTA and Nash-style questions at lower priority. Exam use: The 2025/26 Q4(b) directly asks for the continuous-image theorem and its IVT consequence for 6 marks; the older application families are absent from the latest three papers.

practice.title: Medium/hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Let h:[a,b]→R be continuous and let y lie between h(a) and h(b). The interval [a,b] is connected. Hence h([a,b]) is connected, so it is an interval in R. Because it contains both endpoint values, it contains y. Thus h(c)=y for some c∈[a,b].

practice.title: Graduated exam bridges
practice.prompt: 1. Foundation: Compute χ for a triangle filled by one face. Check: 3−3+1=1; this is older-priority material.
practice.route: 2. Exam style: Let f:[0,1]→[0,1] be continuous. Explain why f has a fixed point. Check: apply IVT to g(x)=f(x)−x; this remains a useful follow-on rather than the exact 2025/26 question.
practice.answer: 2. Exam style: Let f:[0,1]→[0,1] be continuous. Explain why f has a fixed point. Check: apply IVT to g(x)=f(x)−x; this remains a useful follow-on rather than the exact 2025/26 question.

practice.title: Hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: The role of surjectivity in the preservation proof must be explicit. If Y=U∪V is a separation and f:X→Y is onto, then f -1 (U) and f -1 (V) are both nonempty and cover X. Continuity makes them open, so they would separate connected X.

practice.title: Practice question - connected images and IVT [6 marks]
practice.prompt: (a) Let f:X→Y be a continuous surjection. Show that connectedness of X implies connectedness of Y. (b) Briefly explain how this result implies the Intermediate Value Theorem. [6 marks]
practice.route: continuity alone does not make both preimages nonempty; surjectivity is used there.
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: pull a hypothetical separation of Y back to X, then apply the theorem to a continuous real function on an interval.

mistakes: Counting a shared edge twice in a triangulation.
Applying Brouwer when the map does not send the closed ball to itself.
Spending core-revision time on older applications without current lecture evidence.
Calling h([a,b]) an interval without first establishing connectedness.
Recovery rule: Euler's formula uses faces of a particular planar embedding and needs the connected-version constant 2; adjust for disconnected graphs.

sheets.title: Subspaces and Constructions
sheets.purpose: Translate a construction into its defining open sets and then prove the requested property from that definition. Exam use: The 2025/26 paper asks for subspace topology in Q1(c), a 4-mark subspace example in Q1(d), final topology in Q3(a), and two quotient arguments worth 8 marks in Q4(c-d).

practice.title: Medium/hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: The subspace topology on [0,1] inherited from standard R is not discrete. If it were discrete, {1/2} would be open, so {1/2}=[0,1]∩U for some standard-open U⊆R. But any open U containing 1/2 contains an interval around 1/2 and hence other points of [0,1], a contradiction.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridges
practice.prompt: 1. Foundation [4 marks]: Is the standard subspace topology on [0,1] discrete? Check: no; the singleton {1/2} is not relatively open.
practice.route: 2. Exam style [3 marks]: Define the final topology induced on Y by maps f i :X i →Y. Check: U is open exactly when every f i -1 (U) is open; call it the finest such topology.
practice.answer: 2. Exam style [3 marks]: Define the final topology induced on Y by maps f i :X i →Y. Check: U is open exactly when every f i -1 (U) is open; call it the finest such topology.

practice.title: Hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Standard R cannot be a quotient of the Cantor set C. A quotient presentation would supply a continuous surjection q:C→R. Since C is compact, its continuous image q(C)=R would be compact, contradicting the non-compactness of R.

practice.title: Practice question - circle and Cantor quotients [8 marks]
practice.prompt: (a) Briefly explain why S 1 is a quotient of [0,1]. [5 marks] (b) Decide, with justification, whether standard R is a quotient of the Cantor set C. [3 marks]
practice.route: a quotient map is not merely a set-theoretic surjection; use its continuity in the compactness obstruction.
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: for the positive example give the endpoint-identifying quotient map; for the negative example use compactness of continuous images.

mistakes: Using U∩Y but forgetting U must be open in X.
Claiming every subset of a product is a basis element.
Replacing quotient preimages by images.
Recovery rule: The image of an open set under a quotient map need not be open unless its full saturated preimage is open.

sheets.title: Topological Spaces
sheets.purpose: State the topology axioms exactly and distinguish standard, cofinite, discrete, indiscrete and lower-limit examples. Exam use: The 2025/26 paper gives 4 marks for the topology definition, then asks for named topologies and a justified comparison rather than an axiom check on a finite family.

practice.title: Medium/hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: The standard and cofinite topologies on R do not coincide. The interval (0,1) is standard-open, but its complement (-∞,0]∪[1,∞) is infinite, so (0,1) is not cofinite-open. In fact every cofinite-open subset of R is standard-open because a finite subset of R is closed, but the preceding example shows the inclusion is strict.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridges
practice.prompt: 1. Foundation: Is {∅,{a},{b},X} a topology on {a,b}? Check: it is discrete.
practice.route: 2. Exam style: On a finite X with at least two points, show the cofinite topology is discrete. Check: each singleton has finite complement, so is open.
practice.answer: 2. Exam style: On a finite X with at least two points, show the cofinite topology is discrete. Check: each singleton has finite complement, so is open.

practice.title: Hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Describe a basis for the lower-limit topology on R. The answer is the family of half-open intervals [a,b), a<b. Do not replace these by ordinary open intervals: that would generate the standard topology instead.

practice.title: Practice question - definitions and comparison [10 marks]
practice.prompt: (a) Define a topology on a set X. [4 marks] (b) Define the standard topology on R and the cofinite topology on an arbitrary X, then decide with justification whether they coincide on R. [6 marks]
practice.route: “finite intersections” and “arbitrary unions” are not interchangeable, and an unsupported “no” earns less than a concrete separating set.
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: use one mark-bearing clause for each topology axiom, define both named open-set families, then separate them with a standard-open set having infinite complement.

mistakes: Checking only unions of two sets and forgetting the arbitrary-union axiom.
Calling every subset open in the cofinite topology on an infinite set.
Confusing a basis with the full topology.
Recovery rule: A family can pass several sample unions and still fail an arbitrary-union axiom; on finite families, enumerate all distinct unions.
